occurrences: Found in a wide range of igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks, including rhyolite, aplite/granite, gneiss, metapelite, veins, meta-chert, and quartz arenite.
distinguishing: Colorless with 1st-order gray-white interference colors, no cleavage, no alteration or twinning, and commonly shows undulatory (wavy) extinction.
uses: Major silica source for glass, foundry sand, ceramics, silicon metal/semiconductors and aggregate; abundant worldwide, e.g. Brazil, USA (Spruce Pine, North Carolina), Madagascar

occurrences: Found in a wide variety of igneous and metamorphic rocks and, to a lesser extent, in sedimentary rocks.
distinguishing: Colorless with gray-white interference colors; diagnostic sharp polysynthetic albite/pericline twins giving black-and-white zebra-striping in XP, plus concentric zoning.
uses: Mined as feldspar for glass and ceramics; iridescent labradorite/moonstone as ornamental stone; widespread, e.g. USA, Canada (Labrador), Madagascar, Norway

occurrences: Common in many silicic igneous rocks and metamorphosed equivalents; orthoclase/microcline also in high-grade metamorphic rocks and arkoses; sanidine as phenocrysts in rhyolite and trachyte.
distinguishing: Colorless to cloudy/pale-brown with 1st-order gray-white colors and one or two cleavages; orthoclase/sanidine show Carlsbad simple twins and perthite exsolution, microcline shows tartan cross-hatch twinning.
uses: Major feldspar for pottery, porcelain, glass and enamel; mined worldwide, e.g. Turkey, India, Italy, USA (North Carolina, South Dakota)

occurrences: Occurs in Si-poor igneous rocks including syenite (plutonic) and trachyte (volcanic); nepheline foidolites/foidites contain over 60% feldspathoid minerals.
distinguishing: Colorless to cloudy with very low gray-white birefringence, very poor cleavage rarely seen, uniaxial (-); anhedral in plutonics, short prisms or phenocrysts in volcanics.
uses: Nepheline syenite mined as feldspar alternative for glass, ceramics and alumina; Stjernoy, Norway; Kola Peninsula, Russia; Bancroft, Ontario

occurrences: Occurs with nepheline, leucite, or cancrinite in Si-poor alkali-rich igneous rocks and with K-feldspar; especially common in syenites.
distinguishing: Isotropic, colorless to gray (rarely blue) with low relief; mostly anhedral, poor cleavage; darker borders may show cubic cleavage.
uses: Ornamental stone, e.g. Azul Bahia sodalite syenite from Brazil; blue sodalite cut as gem, e.g. Bancroft, Ontario

occurrences: Occurs with nepheline, sodalite, and microcline perthite in Si-poor alkali-rich syenite.
distinguishing: Colorless (slightly clearer than associated nepheline/sodalite) with striking 2nd-order interference colors in XP, uniaxial (-) with lower refractive indices than scapolite.

occurrences: Rare mineral in Si-poor, K-rich igneous rocks, mainly as phenocrysts in lavas; never found with quartz.
distinguishing: Colorless phenocrysts, often 8-sided, with extremely low birefringence appearing almost isotropic, absent/very poor cleavage, and complex polysynthetic twinning in three directions.

occurrences: Mostly metamorphic in marbles, mafic gneisses, and amphibolites, but can also form in alkaline igneous rocks.
distinguishing: Colorless to yellowish rectangular elongate crystals with parallel extinction, uniaxial (-), no twinning, up to 2nd-3rd-order blue interference colors, cleavages at 90 degrees in cross-section.

occurrences: Mafic granulites and ultramafic rocks (orthopyroxenite, websterite) and high-grade metamorphic rocks including garnet amphibolite.
distinguishing: Normally pale with moderate to high relief; low mid- to upper-1st-order interference colors with light-green to pink pleochroism when present, parallel extinction, length-slow.

occurrences: Common in mafic and ultramafic igneous rocks and their high-grade metamorphic equivalents.
distinguishing: High relief, colorless to pale-green or pale-brown with weak pleochroism and middle 2nd-order colors; short prisms with 4- or 8-sided sections, near-orthogonal cleavages, inclined extinction, common twinning.

occurrences: Found in high-grade siliceous marbles and related calcareous metamorphic rocks.
distinguishing: Colorless with high relief, commonly columnar or fibrous aggregates that fracture during thin-sectioning; two good cleavages near 90 degrees, near-parallel extinction, max interference about 1st-order orange.

occurrences: Low-grade mafic metamorphic rocks, commonly with chlorite and epidote in greenschists; tremolite in marbles, calc-silicates, and metamorphosed ultramafic rocks.
distinguishing: Pale yellow-green to slightly blue-green pleochroism (tremolite is the colorless near-end-member of marbles and calc-silicates); moderate-to-high-relief prismatic to fibrous aggregates with amphibole cleavage; 2nd- to lower 3rd-order colors.

occurrences: Found in a wide variety of igneous and metamorphic rocks.
distinguishing: Deep green or brown color with strong pleochroism at moderate-to-high relief; blocky to prismatic crystals with amphibole cleavage; interference colors often masked by the mineral color.

occurrences: Low- to medium-grade Mg-rich metamorphic rocks; anthophyllite is also common in serpentinites.
distinguishing: Colorless anthophyllite to gray-green-tan pleochroic gedrite; moderate-to-high-relief long prisms or fibers with parallel extinction; polysynthetic twins absent (unlike cummingtonite).

occurrences: Some Si-rich volcanic rocks but mostly metamorphosed igneous rocks with hornblende; grunerite in metamorphosed Fe-rich sediments including banded iron formations.
distinguishing: Colorless to pale tan/gray moderate-to-high-relief prisms with inclined extinction and characteristic polysynthetic twinning; 2nd- to lower 3rd-order interference colors.

occurrences: Almost exclusively high-pressure metamorphosed mafic rocks (blueschists and some eclogites); also retrograde alteration of pyroxenes in former eclogites.
distinguishing: Unmistakable blue to lavender pleochroism at moderate-to-high relief; slender prisms with amphibole cleavage; 1st- to lower 2nd-order colors, often anomalous.

occurrences: Found in felsic to intermediate igneous rocks, many metamorphic rocks, and less commonly immature sediments; fine sericite forms by alteration of feldspars.
distinguishing: Almost always colorless mica with moderate relief, tabular crystals or rectangular flakes with one excellent cleavage; up to 2nd-order yellow to red colors, commonly bird's-eye extinction.

occurrences: Occurs in a wide variety of igneous and metamorphic rocks; quite rare in sedimentary rocks except in occasional immature sedimentary rocks.
distinguishing: Typically brown to yellow pleochroic flakes with one excellent cleavage, commonly elongate rectangular; mottled bird's-eye extinction, may hold pleochroic halos around zircon or monazite.

occurrences: Common in low- and medium-grade metamorphic rocks, both as a primary mineral and as a secondary mineral after biotite and other mafic silicates.
distinguishing: Light greenish to army-green, faintly pleochroic patches, flaky or scaly crystals with one excellent cleavage; low 1st-order or anomalous blue, green, purple or brown interference colors.

occurrences: Mostly secondary in mafic and ultramafic igneous rocks by alteration of olivine or pyroxene; also in marbles; forms replacements, aggregates, or veins.
distinguishing: Colorless to green, slightly pleochroic aggregate of small anhedral crystals, often as pseudomorphs with coarse alligator-skin texture; low birefringence, 1st-order gray to yellow; chrysotile is fibrous in veins.

occurrences: A major mineral in some low-grade metamorphic marbles and ultramafic rocks; secondary in altered mafic and ultramafic rocks where found with serpentine.
distinguishing: Colorless sheets in platy masses or fibrous aggregates with subparallel alignment, bent fibers, one good cleavage; 3rd-order pastel patchy colors, diagnostic with marble or ultramafic association.

occurrences: Rare brittle mica of metamorphosed Ca-rich rocks; mentioned only in Sec. 3.6 as resembling muscovite.
Rare brittle mica of contact-metamorphosed limestones and skarns.
Major mineral in many ultramafic and mafic igneous rocks; also in metamorphic mafic gneisses and some marbles and calc-silicates.
distinguishing: Very-high relief, generally colorless (Fe-rich may be faintly yellow pleochroic), typically equant anhedral grains with irregular curved fractures; 2nd-order pastel violet, blue or green colors.

occurrences: Wide variety of metamorphic rocks and some igneous rocks: pyrope in ultramafics, almandine in schists and gneisses, spessartine in granites and pegmatites, grossular/andradite in skarns and marbles.
distinguishing: One of the few common isotropic minerals with high relief, no cleavage but typically fractured, usually very pale pink to tan and nearly always zoned with inclusions; irregular polygons or six-sided euhedral crystals.

occurrences: Widespread accessory mineral in all rock types, generally as tiny grains.
distinguishing: Typically very small uncolored prismatic crystals with pyramidal terminations and very-high relief, extreme birefringence to 4th-order colors; often noticed only by pleochroic halos when included in biotite or chlorite.

occurrences: Often overlooked accessory in many igneous and metamorphic rocks; also in a few sedimentary rocks.
distinguishing: Small grains with very high relief and high-order off-the-chart interference colors; diagnostic diamond, wedge or lenticular euhedral crystals, nearly colorless to light-brown or greenish.

occurrences: Metamorphic mineral common in medium-grade pelitic schists.
distinguishing: High relief with diagnostic pale- to strong-yellow pleochroism, often poikiloblastic with many quartz inclusions (Swiss-cheese texture); euhedral short prisms, max 1st-order yellow to red colors.

occurrences: Common in low- and medium-grade Fe- and Al-rich schists and in high-pressure schists.
distinguishing: Distinctive blue, military green and gray colors in high-relief platy elongate or tabular crystals with pseudohexagonal cross-sections; middle- to upper-1st-order, sometimes anomalous pale-blue colors; polysynthetic twins common.

occurrences: Mainly in low-pressure metamorphosed mudstones and rarely in granites derived from metasedimentary rocks.
distinguishing: Mostly colorless but often with pleochroic pink or rose-red cores, high relief, low-order colors, parallel extinction; euhedral crystals with square cross-sections; dark inclusions may form chiastolite crosses.

occurrences: Primarily in medium- to high-pressure mica schists and gneisses, occasionally in eclogites.
distinguishing: Very high relief broad elongate tabs, laths or blades with one perfect and one good cleavage parallel to length; mostly colorless with upper 1st-order yellow interference colors.

occurrences: High-grade aluminous schists and gneisses.
distinguishing: Colorless high-relief blades or needles with square cross-sections showing a distinctive diagonal cleavage; also fine-grained fibrous masses (fibrolite); up to 2nd-order blue colors.

occurrences: Common in low- and medium-grade greenschists, amphibolites and calc-silicate rocks, and in high-pressure blueschists and eclogites.
distinguishing: Faintly yellowish to pistachio-green epidote while clinozoisite and zoisite are normally colorless, all with high relief; epidote shows intense upper 2nd- to 3rd-order colors, clinozoisite 1st-order, zoisite often anomalous Berlin blue.

occurrences: Rare mineral found primarily in contact aureoles associated with impure limestone or dolomite.
distinguishing: High-relief colorless to light green short tetragonal prisms with rarely visible cleavage; no higher than 1st-order gray colors, commonly with anomalous deep indigo-blue tints.

occurrences: Rare mineral found mainly in high-pressure blueschist-facies metamorphic rocks, less commonly in eclogites.
distinguishing: Colorless subhedral tabular crystals with moderately high relief, typically in blueschists; up to 2nd-order blue colors with rhombic cross-sections and common polysynthetic twins.

occurrences: Common accessory in granitic igneous rocks and many metamorphic rocks, especially mica schists; also major in some pegmatites and clastic sedimentary rocks.
distinguishing: Small strongly colored grains with moderate-to-high relief, stubby prisms with rounded triangular cross sections and no cleavage; brown, green or blue with marked pleochroism, color zoning, reverse absorption.

occurrences: Mostly low-pressure medium- to high-grade regional metamorphism of aluminous rocks; rare in igneous rocks.
distinguishing: Normally colorless with 1st-order gray-white to light-yellow colors; irregular pinching-out polysynthetic twinning, and most distinctively yellow-orange pleochroic halos around zircon or monazite inclusions; common alteration to pinite.

occurrences: Common accessory in metamorphic schists and gneisses and as small grains in intermediate to mafic igneous rocks; less common in veins, pegmatites, and some sediments.
distinguishing: Small prismatic to needle-like crystals with very-high relief and characteristic red to reddish-brown or amber color; extreme birefringence often masked by color, kinked twins in pegmatites.
uses: Titanium ore; Dora Maira Massif, Italy; Beartooth Mountains, Montana; Syros, Greece

occurrences: High-temperature mineral in marbles, metamorphosed marls, schists, or gneisses; also accessory in mafic and ultramafic igneous rocks.
distinguishing: Cubic and isotropic with very high relief, no cleavage, commonly twinned equant octahedral grains; typically colorless to green, brown to reddish-brown, rarely pink or bluish.
uses: Gemstone and refractory; Kilbourne Hole, New Mexico; Pyrenees lherzolite; Montana gneiss

occurrences: Accessory in metamorphosed carbonates, highly aluminous metasediments, some Al-rich igneous rocks, and placers; massive corundum in skarns.
distinguishing: Generally colorless with very high relief and low first-order gray-yellow colors, small rounded grains or zoned hexagonal/tabular crystals; polysynthetic twinning and parting but no good cleavage; colored varieties include sapphire and ruby.
uses: Abrasive and gemstone (ruby, sapphire); Bozeman Corundum Mine, Montana

occurrences: Common accessory in many igneous and metamorphic rocks, often as small colorless grains; fine-grained collophane variety in some sedimentary rocks.
distinguishing: Mostly colorless with moderate relief, typically small stubby prisms with hexagonal cross-section and poor cleavages rarely seen; white to gray interference colors; graphite inclusions may give gray to black hues.
uses: Phosphate fertilizer resource; Phosphoria Formation, Idaho; Cape Verde carbonatite

occurrences: Common accessory in many igneous and metamorphic rocks, often overlooked or mistaken for zircon or titanite.
distinguishing: Small colorless to faintly yellowish grains with very high relief, tiny equant blobs or stubby prisms, very high-order interference colors; radioactive, producing brown halos in biotite/chlorite/hornblende.
uses: Rare-earth and thorium phosphate; Great Smoky Mountains, North Carolina; New Mexico

occurrences: Widespread accessory in schists, marbles, gneisses and other metamorphic rocks; rare in igneous rocks but known from some S-type granites.
distinguishing: Opaque black mineral with metallic luster, small flakes or specks, or sheets interlayered with micas/chlorite; one good cleavage rarely visible.
uses: Industrial carbon (pencils, batteries, lubricants); Beartooth Mountains, Montana; Dutchess County, New York

occurrences: Limestones, dolomites, marbles, marls and calc-silicate rocks, hydrothermal veins, and rare carbonatites; also secondary in many rocks.
distinguishing: Nearly colorless with variable low- to high-relief and perfect rhombohedral cleavage, often twinkling in PP light; almost always polysynthetically twinned with extreme birefringence giving very high-order pastel interference colors.
uses: Limestone/marble building stone and cement; Spergen Limestone, Bedford, Indiana; Adirondack marbles, New York
